pages.summary: A string array of empty strings.
body: Strings (in double quotes) are whole texts held as single elements, where character arrays (in single quotes) are rows of characters. `strings(m, n)` makes an m-by-n array of empty strings to fill in.

examples.title: Filled in a loop

pages.summary: A cell array of character vectors.
body: From a character array, one cell per row with the trailing blanks removed; from a string array, one cell per string; a cell array of text stays as it is.

examples.title: From a padded character array and from strings

pages.summary: Numbers as text: rounded to integers, or a whole matrix in the language's brackets.
body: `int2str` rounds and writes the numbers as `num2str` would; `mat2str` writes a matrix so that evaluating the text gives it back (to 15 significant digits, or `precision`), with `true`/`false` for logical values and quotes for characters.
syntax: To a number of significant digits.

examples.title: Text that evaluates back
examples.code:
int2str([2.4 2.5 -3.7])
s = mat2str([1 2; 3 4.5])
isequal(eval(s), [1 2; 3 4.5])
mat2str(pi, 4)
mat2str([true false])
examples.output:
ans =

    '2  3  -4'

s =

    '[1 2;3 4.5]'

ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

    '3.142'

ans =

    '[true false]'

pages.summary: Text evaluated as an expression, and its value.
body: The text may hold numbers, matrices in brackets and expressions (`'[1 2; 3 4]'`, `'pi/2'`); `ok` is false when it cannot be evaluated. As it evaluates the text, use `str2double` for plain numbers from untrusted text.

examples.title: A matrix, an expression, and text that is not one

pages.summary: Character arrays stacked as rows, padded with spaces, empty ones left out.
body: As `char`, except that empty inputs give no row.

pages.summary: Strings split at a separator or at line breaks, and joined with one; or two tables joined by their keys.
body: `split` splits at white space unless a separator (or several) is given; one string gives a column, several (with the same number of parts) a matrix. `splitlines` splits at line breaks. `join` puts the elements of a string array together with a space or a separator, along the last dimension. For tables, `join(A, B)` adds B's other variables to A, each row matched by its keys.

examples.title: Split and joined again
examples.code:
parts = split("red,green,blue", ",")
join(parts, " / ")
lines = splitlines("first" + newline + "second")
examples.output:
parts =

  3×1 string array

    "red"
    "green"
    "blue"

ans =

    "red / green / blue"

lines =

  2×1 string array

    "first"
    "second"

examples.title: Two tables joined by a key

pages.summary: White space removed from the ends of text.
body: `strtrim` removes leading and trailing white space; `strip` does too, from one side or both, or another character; `deblank` removes trailing white space and null characters only.

examples.title: Three ways of trimming

pages.summary: Spaces: a row of them, text padded with them, and text shifted within its width.
body: `blanks(n)` is a row of n spaces. `pad` pads texts to the longest (or to n) with spaces or another character, on the right unless `'left'` or `'both'`. `strjust` shifts the text of each row of a character array to the right, left or centre within the array's width.

examples.title: A column of names lined up
examples.output:
ans =

  3×1 string array

    "Ada  "
    "Grace"
    "Al   "

ans =

  3×1 string array

    ".....Ada"
    "...Grace"
    "......Al"

ans =

  2×3 char array

    '  a'
    ' bb'

ans =

    '[   ]'

pages.summary: Text backwards.
The number of characters of each string, or of a character vector.

examples.title: Lengths of strings and of text

pages.summary: Texts compared: whole and exact, ignoring case, or by their first n characters.
body: True when the texts are identical (`strcmp`), identical ignoring case (`strcmpi`), or agree in their first n characters (`strncmp`, `strncmpi`). With a cell array or string array, a result for each element; text never equals a number.

examples.title: Four ways of comparing
examples.output:
ans =

  1×3 logical array

   0   1   0

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   1   0

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   0   1   1

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   1   1

pages.summary: Whether text starts with, ends with, or is a pattern (or one of several).
body: The pattern is text, a list of texts (any of which will do), or a pattern object; `'IgnoreCase', true` ignores case.

examples.title: Files by name
examples.output:
ans =

  1×4 logical array

   1   0   1   0

ans =

  1×4 logical array

   1   0   0   1

ans =

  1×4 logical array

   0   1   0   0

pages.summary: Where a pattern occurs in text, and which rows of a list start with some text.
body: `strfind` gives the starting index of every occurrence (overlapping ones too); for a cell array, a cell of them. `strmatch` gives the rows of a character matrix (or elements of a cell array) that start with the text, or with `'exact'` are it.

examples.title: Occurrences, and rows of a list

pages.summary: How many times a pattern occurs in text (occurrences that do not overlap).

examples.title: Letters and words
examples.code:
count("banana", "a")
count(["one two", "three"], " ")
count("Ba ba BA", "ba", 'IgnoreCase', true)

pages.summary: The first token of text, and the rest.
body: Leading delimiters (white space unless given) are skipped; the token runs to the next delimiter, and the rest starts with it.

examples.title: Words one at a time
examples.code:
[t, r] = strtok('  the quick fox')
[t, r] = strtok(r)
[t, r] = strtok('a,b;c', ',;')
examples.output:
t =

    'the'

r =

    ' quick fox'

t =

    'quick'

r =

    ' fox'

t =

    'a'

r =

    ',b;c'

pages.summary: Every occurrence of substrings replaced, or deleted.
body: `replace` takes one old text and one new, or lists of them (each old text its new one); `erase` deletes. Both take patterns too.

examples.title: Replacements and deletions
examples.code:
replace("the cat sat", ["cat" "sat"], ["dog" "ran"])
erase("2026-11-05", "-")
erase("a1b22c333", digitsPattern)

pages.summary: The text before or after a position or a pattern, or between two.
body: The positions are character indices; the patterns texts or pattern objects (the first occurrence counts). `extractBetween` takes `'Boundaries', 'inclusive'` to keep the markers.

examples.title: Parts of a file name and of a tag

pages.summary: The text between two markers or positions replaced, or removed.
body: The markers stay unless `'Boundaries', 'inclusive'` takes them with it.

pages.summary: Text inserted after or before a position or a pattern.
body: At every occurrence of the pattern, or at the character position.

examples.title: A unit and a sign added

pages.summary: Text matched by a regular expression.
body: A regular expression describes text: `\d` a digit, `\w` a word character, `+` one or more, `(...)` a token, `(?<name>...)` a named token. The outputs come in the order of the keywords asked for (`'match'`, `'tokens'`, `'names'`, `'start'`, `'end'`, `'split'`); without keywords, the starting indices. `'once'` gives the first match only, not in a cell. `regexpi` ignores case.

examples.title: Numbers, named parts and splits
examples.code:
s = 'x = 12, y = 345, z = 6';
regexp(s, '\d+', 'match')
d = regexp('2026-11-05', '(?<year>\d+)-(?<month>\d+)-(?<day>\d+)', 'names')
regexp('a1b22c', '\d+', 'split')
regexpi('Hello HELLO hello', 'hello', 'match')
examples.output:
ans = 

  1×3 cell array

    {'12'}    {'345'}    {'6'}

d = 

  struct with fields:

     year: '2026'
    month: '11'
      day: '05'

ans = 

  1×3 cell array

    {'a'}    {'b'}    {'c'}

ans = 

  1×3 cell array

    {'Hello'}    {'HELLO'}    {'hello'}

pages.summary: The matches of a regular expression replaced.
body: In the replacement, `$1`, `$2`, ... stand for the tokens; `'once'` replaces the first match only, `'ignorecase'` ignores case.

pages.summary: Text escaped for use in a regular expression, or a wildcard turned into one.
body: `'escape'` puts a backslash before each character that has a meaning in a regular expression; `'wildcard'` turns `*` and `?` into `.*` and `.`, as file names are matched.
syntax: A wildcard as a regular expression.

examples.title: A literal dot, and a file mask
examples.code:
e = regexptranslate('escape', 'a.b')
regexp('axb a.b', e, 'match')
w = regexptranslate('wildcard', '*.csv')
regexp({'a.csv', 'b.txt'}, ['^' w '$'], 'match', 'once')
examples.output:
e =

    'a\.b'

ans = 

  1×1 cell array

    {'a.b'}

w =

    '.*\.csv'

ans = 

  1×2 cell array

    {'a.csv'}    {''}

pages.summary: Which characters are white space, letters, or of another category.
body: `isstrprop(s, category)` tests for `'alpha'`, `'digit'`, `'alphanum'`, `'upper'`, `'lower'`, `'wspace'`, `'punct'`, `'cntrl'` or `'xdigit'`, a result for each character.

examples.title: The characters of a short text
examples.output:
ans =

  1×5 logical array

   0   0   1   0   0

ans =

  1×5 logical array

   1   1   0   0   0

ans =

  1×5 logical array

   0   0   0   1   0

ans =

  1×5 logical array

   0   0   0   0   1

pages.summary: Whether a value is text: a character array or a string array; and whether it is a single string.
syntax: A char array or a string array.

examples.title: Text, and not
examples.output:
ans =

  1×4 logical array

   1   1   0   0

ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   0   0

pages.summary: Integers in binary, hexadecimal or another base, and back.
body: `dec2bin`, `dec2hex` and `dec2base` (bases 2 to 36) write nonnegative integers as digits, at least `n` of them when given; several numbers give rows of the same width. A negative number is written in two's complement. `bin2dec`, `hex2dec` and `base2dec` read the digits back.

examples.title: The same numbers in three bases
examples.code:
dec2bin([5 12], 8)
bin2dec('1100')
dec2hex(255)
hex2dec('FF')
dec2base(35, 36)
base2dec('Z', 36)
dec2bin(-1, 8)

pages.summary: A double's IEEE 754 bits as 16 hexadecimal digits, and a double from them.
body: The sign, exponent and fraction of a double, as stored; useful to see exactly which number a value is.

pages.summary: The line feed character, char(10).
Formatted data read from text.
body: The format is applied again and again until the text is used up or does not match: `%d` and `%f` numbers, `%s` a word (as its character codes in a numeric result), literal text to match. The numbers come as a column unless `sizeA` gives a shape; `count` is how many were read.
syntax: With how many, any error, and where reading stopped.

examples.title: Numbers out of a line of text

pages.summary: The valid text that a text abbreviates, or an error.
body: Matches ignore case and may be the start of a valid text; when the text starts more than one valid text that are not prefixes of one another, or none, it is an error. Made for checking options given to a function.

examples.title: An option given short
examples.code:
opts = {'linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'};
validatestring('cub', opts)
validatestring('NEAR', opts)
try, validatestring('spline', opts); catch e, disp(e.message), end
examples.output:
ans =

    'cubic'

ans =

    'nearest'

Expected input to match one of these values:

'linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'

The input, 'spline', did not match any of the valid values.

pages.summary: Inputs converted between character vectors and strings; anything else passed through.
body: For functions that take either kind of text: convert once at the start, work with one kind, and give the other back if wanted. Cells of character vectors become string arrays and string arrays become cells of character vectors.

examples.title: Mixed inputs made one kind
examples.output:
a =

    "abc"

b =

  1×2 string array

    "x"    "y"

c =

     5

ans =

    'abc'

pages.summary: Bytes as Base64 text, and back.
body: Base64 writes bytes with 64 printable characters, four for every three bytes, so binary data can travel as text. Text is encoded as UTF-8 first; decoding gives a uint8 row.

examples.title: Text there and back
examples.output:
b =

    'aGVsbG8='

v =

  1×5 uint8 row vector

   104   101   108   108   111

ans =

    'hello'

pages.summary: Text as the bytes of an encoding, and bytes as text.
body: UTF-8 unless an encoding is named (`'ISO-8859-1'`, `'windows-1252'`, `'UTF-16'`, ...). A character the encoding lacks becomes `?`; bytes that do not decode become U+FFFD.

examples.title: The same letter in two encodings
examples.output:
ans =

  1×2 uint8 row vector

   195   164

ans =

  uint8

   228

ans =

    'ä'

pages.summary: Text wrapped to a width.
body: Each paragraph (a cell element, a string, or a line) is broken at spaces into lines of at most `columns` characters (a longer word gets a line of its own), as a column cell array. With a uicontrol, the width comes from the control.

examples.title: A sentence in lines of 20
examples.code: c = textwrap({'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.'}, 20)
